answer: GPUs, NPUs, TPUs, chip fabs, memory and storage, plus the datacenters, power, cooling, and networking underneath them.

reading.body:
The AI hardware stack is organized into six layers, and the data counts them unevenly: accelerators, fabrication, memory, and networking, with no entries yet under datacenters, power, or cooling.

The six built sections are GPUs, NPUs and TPUs, chip fabrication, memory and storage, memory supply, and networking fabric. Their entry counts are 6, 7, 5, 4, an unstated number, and 5. Memory supply is the only section without a count, which suggests it is a narrative or explainer rather than an index of parts. The blurbs describe two distinct fabrics, scale-up within a rack and scale-out between racks, which is the layer that determines whether accelerators can be pooled into one training job.

For AI specifically, the structure implies that capability is assembled from separately sourced pieces: silicon from fabs, memory from a small supplier base, and interconnect that binds racks together. The memory supply blurb is the only place the data names a concrete pressure, that memory pricing is untracked by any index and feeds through to PC memory prices. That is a supply-chain observation, not a compute one, and it is the closest this data comes to the thesis that hardware availability, not model design, sets the ceiling.

What the data does not cover is the part of its own blurb about datacenters, power, and cooling. Those appear in the description but have no section and no count. So this is a map of the silicon and interconnect layers, and the facilities and electricity underneath them are asserted but not yet populated. Nothing here gives dates, capacities, or vendors, so no trend can be read from it.

items.claim: Groq and NVIDIA entered a non-exclusive licensing agreement for Groq's inference technology, with Groq's founder and other leaders joining NVIDIA while Groq stayed independent.

AMD and OpenAI agreed a partnership for up to 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct accelerators, the first gigawatt from the second half of 2026, with OpenAI receiving a warrant for AMD shares tied to milestones.
HPE and NVIDIA announced NVIDIA AI Computing by HPE, a jointly built private AI stack combining NVIDIA GPUs and AI Enterprise software with HPE GreenLake.
